title: Building and running your code
summary: Start, watch it build, read the console, then enable the robot.

say.never: The strip at the bottom of the screen is your **Driver Station**. Think of it as the remote control for your robot: it's where you start your code and drive the pretend robot on the screen. A real team has one on a laptop at every match.
say.bit: This strip at the bottom is your **Driver Station**. It's how you build your code, run it in the simulator, and control the robot, just like the laptop at a real match.

say.never: Before you start the robot, look for **red squiggly lines** in your code. Those are mistakes, like a spelling error. The editor counts them here. Fix every one first, because code with a mistake can't start.
say.bit: If the editor finds a mistake, it underlines it in red and counts it down here. Fix those first, because code with errors won't build.

say.never: Press **Start**. It does two things for you. First it **builds** your code, which means turning the Java you typed into something the computer can run. Then it **runs** it on the pretend robot.
say.bit: **Start** does two things: it **builds** your code (turns your Java into something the robot can run), then **runs** it in the simulator.

say.never: This tells you what's happening: **Building**, then **Running**. The very first build is slow, so be patient. After that it's much quicker.
say.bit: This shows where it's up to: **Building**, then **Running**. The first build takes the longest, and later ones are quicker.

say.never: This is the **console**, where your code can write messages for you to read. If something goes wrong when building, the explanation shows up here. Look for a **file name and a line number**. That tells you exactly where to look.
say.bit: Everything your code prints with `System.out.println` shows up here. So do build errors: if the build fails, look here for the **file name and line number** it's unhappy about.

say.never: Choose what the robot should do. **Teleop** means *you* drive it with the keyboard. **Auto** means it drives itself with no help. **Test** is for trying things. For now, pick **Teleop**.
say.bit: Pick what the robot should do: **Teleop** (you drive), **Auto** (it drives itself), or **Test**.

say.never: Your robot starts **disabled**, which is like a car with the engine off. Nothing moves until you press **Enable**. **Disable** stops everything right away, so it's your safety button. Real robots work the same way.
say.bit: Robot code starts **disabled**, so nothing moves until you say so. Press **Enable** to let it run, and **Disable** to stop it at once. Same as a real robot.

say.never: Changed your code? Press **Restart**. It builds your new code and runs it again. **Stop** just ends the run.
say.bit: After you change your code, press **Restart**. It builds the new version and runs it. **Stop** ends the run.
